newsitem.title: FRANCE: Yield fears grow in third French durum region.
newsitem.headline: Yield fears grow in third French durum region.

text.p: Grain crop analysts in Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur, the Mediterranean region stretching north from Marseille in southeastern France, say drought damage to the durum crop may be worse than feared.

With a small part of the harvest already in, official analysts said the latest local projection of a 21 percent drop in yields could have to be revised as more of the shrivelled crop is weighed and assessed at silos.

The region -- France's third largest for durum wheat -- was among the worst affected by the second spring drought in two years. Although water deficits between January and April may have been worse in northwestern France, those areas recovered well after ample rain in May and most of northern France expects a strong grain crop this year.
Farmers in Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur planted 56,000 hectares of durum this year, up slightly from last year's 54,795. Regional sowings are 22 percent of France's total.

Government crop officials said their latest yield forecast from the region was 2.5 tonnes a hectare, down 21 percent from 3.175 tonnes last year. Because of the slightly higher area sowed, that would suggest a 20 percent drop in production to 140,000 tonnes.

But analysts said evidence from individual farms showed an astonishing variety in yields from an above-average 4.5 tonnes all the way down to zero, and many farmers were reporting yields in a range of 1.5 to 2.0 tonnes a hectare.

"The yield forecasts are probably going to come down. It has been a particularly bad year -- really it could not have been worse," regional crop official said. Another predicted output in several areas would be broadly halved, but cautioned this was still provisional.
One part of the region, the north of Vaucluse province near the Rhone river, even suffered a small tornado in the past week, destroying several square kilometres of crops.

The odd-seeming concept of a zero yield is due to the fact that some farmers in worst-hit areas will not bother to harvest durum this year, one crop official said. The cost of bringing out the combine harvesters would wipe out the value of the grain, he said.

It was not clear how many farmers were in such dire straits, nor what compensation, if any, they would get. But many farmers and co-operatives are expected to face some financial difficulty this year. Silo managers fear volumes will plummet.
On a more positive note, some farmers who had access to water supplies were expected to manage near-normal yields of 4.5 tonnes this year and crop quality was generally high.
Test weight on volumes seen so far was better than expected, at 78 or 80 kilos per hectolitre compared with 83 or 85 for an average-to-good year, analysts said.

But the growth of secondary shoots was sharply reduced because roots had not developed well enough to tap the soil for moisture which arrived in late spring. So the number of wheat ears per hectare will be significantly below normal.
The five-year regional yield for 1992-96, calculated by Reuters from national data, is 3.33 tonnes a hectare. --Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5452
